content:
A couple new features have been recently added to the Live Lean playground at live.lean-lang.org, including Cslib support for the latest stable and beta releases.

Today we’re also adding a feature that makes the Comparator tool, our trustworthy judge for Lean proofs from untrusted sources or AI actors, easier to access. Comparator is described as our “gold standard” in our guide to Validating a Lean Proof, and it powers our “lean-eval” AI Formalization Leaderboard.

Starting today, if you follow a Zulip link to an AI-generated proof of the finite Ramsey theorem for graphs (this example via rkirov on githubv), you’ll get a new warning to not necessarily trust claims about the significance of Lean developments that come from random Zulip links without validation from Comparator. Clicking “Can I Trust This Proof?” takes you to Comparator Live, where you can select “Finite Ramsey theorem for graphs” from the drop-down menu, and hit Run Verification. Comparator will verify that the proof proves a known version of the theorem, using only Lean’s standard axioms.

This is amazing!! Is there any way to prepare GitHub repos in some sort of standard way so we can provide a link for users use the publicly available comparator website?

This is something we'd have loved for putting AI-generated lean verifications on arXiv (like https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20527). We can explain the Lean to the reader like we do in the last section, and write a comparator that contains exactly the same code we explain in the paper, but it would be lovely to have a link for people to run the check automatically.

@Jaume de Dios I do have a sketch of a design that would let you point comparator live at a GitHub link that contains a lean-toolchain, a Challenge.lean, and a Solution.lean, and load the development with the best option available. So in that sense the answer to your question is “just have two files that only depend on Mathlib named Challenge.lean and Solution.lean”, and your ask makes me more likely to get around to implementing that when I have a chance!

The main gotcha there is that comparator projects track live.lean-lang.org project versions, and are only available for Latest Mathlib, Latest Release (currently v4.32.0-rc1), and Stable Release (currently v4.31.0). But those projects drift forward, so your development might not continue to work in a future lean version. It’s not reliably archival, in other words.

I do think there’s a need for “standards for comparator in artifact evaluation” that you’re gesturing at and I’ve got half a mind to write one.

That is really great to hear! How do you feel (temporarily maybe?) as a simpler system where one "archives" the comparator output, together with the reasonable metadata? Some sort of stored snapshots associated to a particular commit. This also lightens the load for heavier projects.

My motivation for not caching completed verification information is mostly to give a realistic picture of how comparator works — it's not instantaneous and can be stately for large projects, it's engineered to be reliable not fast. We would change that decision if load becomes an issue.

Archiving successful verification longer-term raises a couple of concerns: not just reliably maintaining data but also thinking through privacy concerns. All these are things I think we could solve it there's appetite for it in the community, though! But at some level there's a solution for heavier projects — it's comparator the command line tool
